sets.title: Meaning
sets.summary: Whether life has a point, and who gets to decide what it is.

questions.statement: If nothing you do will matter in a million years, nothing you do matters now.
Life has no meaning except the meaning each person gives it.
Someone rolling the same rock up the same hill forever could have a meaningful life, if they loved doing it.
Some lives are more meaningful than others, whatever the people living them think.
A contented life spent counting blades of grass is as good as a life spent curing diseases.
Most people drift through life without ever really choosing how to live.
When people say they had no choice, they are almost always deceiving themselves.
Without God, life would have no ultimate meaning.
A life without any suffering could never be deeply meaningful.
You are avoiding what you already know would make your life more meaningful.
A life given over to one great work is better than a balanced, ordinary one.
The most important choices in life can only be made by a leap that reason cannot justify.
Most people would be happier if the shape of their lives had been chosen for them.
There is a human nature that tells each of us how we ought to live.
You are nothing more than what you do.

sets.title: Nihilism and Value
sets.summary: Whether anything is really good or bad, and what makes it so.

questions.statement: Things matter only because someone cares about them.
A universe with no conscious beings in it would contain nothing of value.
A world with no suffering at all would be worse than ours.
Pleasure is the only thing that is good for its own sake.
If a machine could give you a lifetime of perfectly simulated happiness, plugging in for good would be the wise choice.
Every claim that something is good or bad is, strictly speaking, false.
Once belief in God fades, people's values have nothing left to stand on.
People who believe nothing matters are more likely to do harm.
Realising that nothing ultimately matters would set you free.
For most people, life holds more suffering than happiness.
Some things are beautiful whether or not anyone finds them so.
A short life of deep understanding is worth more than a long life of simple pleasures.
Your deepest values are no more correct than the opposite values someone else holds.
Since evolution shaped what we value, our values tell us nothing about what is really good.
Humility is a virtue invented by the weak to hold back the strong.

sets.title: Morality
sets.summary: What makes actions right or wrong, and how much morality can ask of you.

questions.statement: Pushing one stranger in front of a runaway train is right if it saves five others.
Lying is wrong even when it would save an innocent life.
Not giving to effective charities is as wrong as letting a child drown in front of you.
Morality never requires you to give up your own life plans for the sake of strangers.
A drunk driver who kills a child is no more to blame than an equally drunk driver who gets home safely.
Whether an action is wrong depends on the culture it happens in.
Some moral claims are as true as the claims of mathematics.
You should save your own child over two strangers' children.
Whether an act was right depends only on its results.
Letting someone die is just as bad as killing them.
Most people's moral views are just the views of the people they grew up around.
Most people would behave badly if they knew they could never be caught.
When a moral theory clashes with a strong gut feeling, you should trust the theory.
Being a good person matters more than doing the right thing.
Wrongdoers deserve to suffer, even when their suffering does no one any good.

sets.title: Mind and Self
sets.summary: Free will, consciousness, and what makes you the same person over time.

questions.statement: We have free will.
If every choice is caused by things outside your control, no one truly deserves blame.
You act freely whenever you do what you want, even if what you want was fixed before you were born.
Consciousness is entirely a matter of physical processes in the brain.
Science will one day fully explain why it feels like something to be you.
A being could act exactly like you in every way and still feel nothing at all.
A computer program could one day genuinely feel pain.
An AI that talks about its feelings as convincingly as a person probably has some.
You would still be you if every one of your memories were replaced.
A teleporter that destroys your body and builds an exact copy elsewhere would carry you, not kill you.
There is no self, only a stream of thoughts and feelings.
Someone with advanced dementia is, in the ways that matter, no longer the person they were.
Some form of experience is present in all matter, down to the smallest particles.
You often have no idea why you really do what you do.
Each person has a soul that is distinct from their body.

sets.title: God and Religion
sets.summary: Whether God exists, and what faith, morality and religion have to do with each other.

questions.statement: God exists.
The amount of suffering in the world shows there is no all-good, all-powerful God.
A world of free creatures who can do great evil is better than a world of creatures who always do good.
The universe's fitness for life is best explained by a designer.
No report of a miracle could ever give you good reason to believe one happened.
Without God, there would be no objective morality.
If God commanded cruelty, cruelty would be right.
Believing in God without evidence can be rational.
If you are unsure whether God exists, the wise bet is to believe.
Since most people's religion depends on where they were born, no religion can claim to be the true one.
All the major religions are different paths to the same truth.
A loving God would make sure no one could honestly doubt that God exists.
Religion has done more harm than good in human history.
A powerful experience of God's presence gives the person who has it good reason to believe.
Atheism takes as much faith as religion does.

sets.title: Knowledge and Truth
sets.summary: What you can know, how you can know it, and whom to trust.

questions.statement: You can be certain that the world around you is real.
It is more likely than not that we live in a computer simulation.
Science is the only reliable way to find out what is true.
Something can be true for one person and false for another.
It is wrong to believe anything without enough evidence.
When someone as smart and informed as you disagrees, you should become less sure.
We have no rational basis for expecting the sun to rise tomorrow.
Our best scientific theories are close to the literal truth about the world.
Believing something because experts say so is not really knowing it.
Nothing can be known with complete certainty.
Some truths about the world can be known by reason alone, without any experience.
Believing something false can be the right choice when it makes your life better.
You know your lottery ticket will lose before the draw.
Philosophy has never settled any of its big questions.
People who suffer an injustice understand it better than anyone studying it from outside.
Experts are wrong far more often than they admit.

sets.title: Liberty
sets.summary: How free people should be, and when society may step in.

questions.statement: The state may stop you from doing something only if it harms other people.
Adults should be free to take any drug, however dangerous, as long as they only risk themselves.
Governments should quietly steer people toward better choices, as long as they can still choose otherwise.
Speech that is hateful but not threatening should be legal.
Mocking what others hold sacred is wrong, even when it is legal.
A tolerant society has the right to suppress intolerant views.
The state should stay neutral about what makes a good life.
Some things should be illegal simply because they are immoral, even if they harm no one.
Someone too poor to act on their choices is not really free.
A slave with a kind master who never interferes is still unfree.
You should be allowed to sell yourself into lifelong servitude if you freely choose to.
Giving up some privacy for greater safety is usually a good trade.
Cultural groups can have rights that their individual members do not.
Most people would be better off living under firmer rules.
People should be exempt from laws that go against their religious conscience.

sets.title: Politics and Power
sets.summary: Who has the right to rule, and how wealth and power should be shared.

questions.statement: You have a moral duty to obey the law even when you think it is wrong.
No state has ever had the right to rule anyone.
Living in a country and using its services counts as agreeing to its laws.
Votes should count for more when the voter knows more.
A wise ruler who governed well would be better than a democracy that governed badly.
Large inequalities of wealth are unjust, however they came about.
Taxing people's earnings is a kind of forced labour.
A fair society is one you would choose to live in without knowing where in it you would end up.
Markets decide who gets what more fairly than any government could.
Private ownership of land is fundamentally unjust.
Violent revolution can be justified against a government that was fairly elected.
Behind every claim to serve the common good is someone's bid for power.
A good ruler must be willing to deceive the public.
A nation has the right to decide who may live within its borders.
You owe more to your fellow citizens than to people in other countries.

sets.title: Society and Culture
sets.summary: Tradition and progress, family and identity, and what technology is doing to us.

questions.statement: Long-standing traditions usually contain wisdom, even when no one can say what it is.
Humanity is morally better now than it has ever been.
Talented people do not deserve the rewards their talents bring.
Parents have the right to raise their children in their own values, even ones the rest of society rejects.
You owe your parents care in their old age, whatever kind of parents they were.
Who you are is mostly shaped by the groups you belong to.
Most differences between how men and women behave are learned rather than innate.
Modern technology has made human life worse in the ways that matter most.
Parents should be allowed to choose genes that make their children smarter.
Borrowing from another culture's traditions without permission can be wrong.
Some cultures are better than others.
People were happier in simpler, pre-industrial societies.
Societies need shame to keep people behaving well.
Modern societies value individual freedom more than is good for them.
Popular culture mostly works to keep people passive.

sets.title: Life and Death
sets.summary: Death, who should exist, which lives count, and how much the future matters.

questions.statement: Death is nothing to fear, since once you are dead there is no you left to suffer.
Dying young is a misfortune even for someone who never knew what they were missing.
Living forever would eventually make life unbearable.
Doctors should be allowed to help terminally ill patients end their lives when they ask.
Every human life is equally valuable, whatever its quality.
Bringing a new person into existence always harms them.
Eating animals is wrong when there are good alternatives.
A pig's suffering matters as much as the same suffering in a human.
People who will live a thousand years from now matter as much as people alive today.
Human extinction would be bad even if it happened painlessly.
A vast population of people whose lives are barely worth living could be better than a small, flourishing one.
A fetus has the same moral status as a newborn baby.
Some crimes are so terrible that the people who commit them deserve to die.
When you die, you cease to exist forever.
We should reduce the suffering of wild animals, even if it means interfering with nature.
